title: Functional ice cream development with ingredient substitution and bioactive enrichment
abstract: Abstract This review article discusses recent advances in the reformulation of ice cream, focusing on the transformation of this traditional product into a functional food. The analysis covers the substitution of conventional ingredients, including dairy proteins, fats, sugars, and synthetic emulsifiers, with plant-based, natural, and bioactive alternatives, aiming to meet the growing demand for healthier, more sustainable, and clean-label products. Publications from the past five years were considered, addressing dairy substitutes (soy, almond, hazelnut, sheep milk), fat replacers based on fibers and proteins, natural sweeteners (stevia, honey, fruit syrups), and natural emulsifiers (gums, pectins, plant proteins). In addition to structural substitutions, the study highlights the role of functional supplements, probiotics, prebiotics, antioxidants, vitamins, and natural colorants, in improving the nutritional value and health-promoting potential of the final product. Evidence indicates that it is possible to develop ice creams with enhanced nutritional profiles, functional properties, and physicochemical stability, although the challenge of preserving texture and sensory acceptance remains. The review proposes that hybrid formulation strategies, combining plant-based ingredients, bioactives, and sensory optimization techniques, represent a promising pathway for establishing ice cream as a functional matrix and a vehicle for bioactive compounds.
journal: Journal of Food Science and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The food industry has increasingly invested in innovations that balance health, sustainability, and sensory pleasure, with ice cream being one of the most challenging products for reformulation due to its complex multiphase structure (Raisel et al.  58 ). It is an emulsion composed of air, ice crystals, and fat droplets dispersed in a partially frozen matrix, whose stability depends on precise control of ingredients and processing conditions (Codex Alimentarius  7 ; Čolić et al.  43 ).

Studies show that replacing conventional ingredients directly affects physicochemical and sensory properties. Bioactive compounds can modify emulsion stability (Gouda et al.  19 ), while stabilizers influence viscosity and freezing behavior Góral et al. ( 17 ). Hydrocolloids improve texture in low-fat formulations, although their performance depends on concentration and system interactions (Javidi et al.  32 ). Sugar replacement, despite nutritional benefits, often compromises sensory acceptance (Genovese et al.  13 ).

Despite advances in functional and plant-based formulations, the literature still treats these topics in a fragmented way (Genovese et al.  13 ; Issazadeh and Hatami  27 ), limiting an integrated understanding of combined effects. Mohammed et al. ( 47 ) highlight that adding functional ingredients improves nutritional value, but technological and sensory challenges remain.

The concept of functional foods has evolved to include health benefits beyond basic nutrition (Sarkar  66 ), and organizations such as FAO and WHO encourage the incorporation of bioactive compounds into dairy products. In this context, ice creams enriched with probiotics, fibers, antioxidants, and other compounds represent a promising strategy to transform them into functional food matrices.

Current research also prioritizes sustainable and clean-label substitutions, using natural and recognizable ingredients to increase consumer acceptance (Loffredi and Alamprese  40 ; Paglia et al.  55 ). Additionally, there is a trend toward multifunctional ingredients that simultaneously contribute to structure, stability, and bioactivity.

Plant proteins and fibers show potential to replace traditional components but still face challenges in texture and stability (Gorman et al.  18 ). Sugar replacement remains one of the major challenges due to its multifunctional role, and alternatives such as stevia and xylitol often introduce undesirable sensory effects (Genovese et al.  13 ). Natural emulsifiers and stabilizers also present limitations in cost and scalability (Loffredi et al.  41 ; Qin et al.  57 ).

The incorporation of bioactive compounds such as prebiotic fibers, antioxidants, and vitamins is driving the transformation of ice cream into a functional matrix with potential metabolic and gut health benefits (Sarkar  66 ). However, important sensory limitations still persist, especially in plant-based formulations (Genovese et al.  13 ).

Therefore, this review adopts an integrated approach combining ingredient substitution and bioactive enrichment, highlighting synergistic strategies to simultaneously improve nutritional value, technological functionality, and sensory quality, positioning ice cream as a promising functional food matrix.

sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: A literature review was conducted to identify studies on functional ice cream development, focusing on ingredient substitution and bioactive enrichment. Searches were performed in Google Scholar, ResearchRabbit, and Lens.org between August and October 2025, using keywords related to ice cream reformulation and functional ingredients combined with Boolean operators.

Articles published within the last five years were prioritized. Inclusion criteria included original, full-text English articles related to ice cream formulation and functionality, while exclusions covered duplicates, abstracts, incomplete papers, and unrelated studies. The selected literature was then qualitatively analyzed to support discussion on ingredient substitution and functional enhancement strategies in ice cream systems.

sections.heading: Substitutes in ice cream
paragraphs: Individuals with lactose intolerance, high cholesterol, or milk allergies increasingly shift toward plant-based alternatives, a trend also driven by vegetarian and vegan lifestyles (Atalar et al.  2 ). Ice cream’s structure directly influences its rheological behavior and melting properties. While ice phases determine viscosity, other components, such as partially coalesced fat globules, overrun, and the unfrozen serum phase, affect melting resistance and texture (Freire et al.  12 ). Fat destabilization alters both sensory qualities and melt resistance, while stabilizers help control ice recrystallization and improve product consistency (Freire et al.  12 ; Loffredi et al.  41 ; Raisel et al.  58 ). The mixture’s viscosity, in turn, impacts overall mouthfeel and rheology (Freire et al.  12 ).

However, removing or substituting any single ingredient can compromise product stability and sensory appeal, risking consumer rejection (Nwaogazie et al.  53 ). To counterbalance these effects, fruits, seeds, or other functional components may be added to reinforce formulation quality, provided they preserve texture and flavor (da Silva et al.  8 ; Genovese et al.  13 ). The dual sensory and nutritional appeal of ice cream makes it attractive to consumers seeking both enjoyment and health benefits, though maintaining desirable texture and flavor is essential for acceptance (Genovese et al.  13 ).

Ice cream is globally recognized as a pleasurable frozen product composed of milk, sugars, stabilizers, emulsifiers, and flavorings, sometimes with additional ingredients such as eggs or starch hydrolysates (Thampitak et al.  72 ; Raisel et al.  58 ). Its production involves mixing, pasteurization, homogenization, aging, dynamic freezing, packaging, and hardening. During freezing, air incorporation (overrun), crystal formation, and fat dispersion create the characteristic smooth and soft texture of this multiphase system (Thampitak et al.  72 ; Li et al.  81 ). Each processing step, from pasteurization to flavor addition, is carefully designed to optimize quality, with key sensory attributes such as overrun, firmness, and melting behavior determining consumer acceptance (Loffredi and Alamprese  40 ).

Different reformulation strategies present distinct advantages and limitations. While fat replacers are often associated with greater impacts on texture and mouthfeel, sugar substitutes primarily affect sweetness perception and freezing behavior. Similarly, plant-based formulations offer sustainability benefits but frequently require technological adjustments to match the sensory properties of dairy systems. Encapsulation strategies, although effective in improving stability and bioavailability, may increase formulation complexity and cost. Therefore, selecting an appropriate strategy depends on balancing nutritional goals, technological feasibility, and sensory acceptance.

sections.heading: Dairy substitutes
paragraphs: Conventional ice cream typically contains 3.5–4% (w/w) milk protein, which plays a crucial role due to its emulsifying, foaming, and water-holding properties (Roy et al.  63 ). These proteins interact with emulsifiers at the fat–water interface, stabilizing fat droplets and contributing to foam structure and air bubble stability. They also enhance viscosity in the unfrozen phase, reducing ice crystal formation and improving shape retention, fat destabilization, and melting behavior (Detoni et al.  10 ).

Lactose provides sweetness and lowers the freezing point of ice cream (Roy et al.  63 ),, while milk enzymes help stabilize air cells within the matrix (Hanafi et al.  22 ). However, growing rates of lactose intolerance and milk allergies, affecting up to 70% of the global population, have increased demand for non-dairy alternatives. Consequently, plant-based milks such as soy, coconut, and almond have gained popularity as ingredients in vegan and functional ice creams. This shift is also influenced by factors such as limited milk availability, high prices, and health concerns associated with contaminated dairy products (Balthazar et al.  5 ).

Consumer acceptance depends heavily on sensory attributes. Preference is generally higher for ice creams with creamy flavor, soft texture, and buttery mouthfeel, while awareness of a plant-based origin often reduces perceived quality (Gorman et al.  18 ). Sheep’s milk offers a nutritious, hypoallergenic alternative to bovine milk, with higher dry matter and greater concentrations of essential vitamins and minerals (Balthazar et al.  5 ; Kowalczyk et al.  34 ).

Although research into plant-based ice creams is advancing, issues related to stability, texture, nutrition, and sensory quality remain. Replacing cow’s milk with alternatives such as soy, coconut, or watermelon seed milk can enhance nutritional and functional properties (Atalar et al.  2 ). To achieve desirable quality, formulations should match the viscosity of milk-based mixes and promote partial fat coalescence, ensuring stable foam structure and slow melting. Combining different plant-based milks can optimize their individual properties and improve texture and sensory performance (Taspinar et al.  71 ).

Animal-derived milk remains the preferred option due to its superior emulsification capacity and higher protein content, while plant-based milks align with the growing demand for sustainable and vegan products. However, they present challenges such as lower protein concentration and weaker emulsifying ability. This highlights the need for technological innovation to reconcile consumer expectations with sustainability goals.

Several studies have explored milk substitutes in ice cream, ranging from animal sources (sheep, camel) to plant-based beverages (soy, almond, hazelnut, hemp), according Table  1 . These alternatives display distinct functional and sensory characteristics, influenced by their compositional diversity.

For instance, soluble rice extract with prebiotics increased antioxidant activity (da Silva et al.  8 ), while symbiotic sheep milk ice cream demonstrated chemopreventive effects (Balthazar et al.  5 ). Adding apple fiber reduced melting time but negatively affected texture and appearance (Kowalczyk et al.  34 ). Hazelnut milk improved protein content and antioxidant capacity, achieving high sensory acceptance at up to 75% substitution (Atalar et al.  2 ).

Other formulations showed promising results: almond and hemp milk ice creams varied in solids and fat content, with hemp preferred by consumers (Leahu et al.  39 ); coconut-based products received positive feedback (Kasapoglu et al.  33 ); olive oil substitution improved antioxidant potential without compromising sensory quality (Tagliamonte et al.  69 ); and camel milk combined with black rice enhanced texture and melting resistance (Elkot et al.  11 ). Soy and lupin protein also improved nutritional profiles, although traditional samples remained more acceptable (Hasan et al.  24 ).

Comparative analyses indicate that soy protein is the most balanced alternative to milk protein, combining good stability, slow melting, and high sensory acceptance. Pea protein offers strong structural stability but a firmer texture and distinct flavor, while brown rice protein, despite higher overrun, melts faster and has lower sensory appeal (Hasan et al.  24 ). Blends of soy, rice, and apple fibers can enhance melting resistance and aeration, while combinations like almond milk with psyllium and coconut pulp have shown favorable texture and sensory results (Leahu et al.  39 ).

Overall, ice creams formulated with ingredients such as camel milk or black rice exhibit enhanced antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, positioning them as functional alternatives with health potential (Elkot et al.  11 ). However, despite nutritional and functional gains, maintaining balance between stability, appearance, and sensory quality remains the key challenge. Continuous optimization of plant-based formulations is necessary to achieve sensory parity with traditional dairy ice creams while preserving their functional and nutritional advantages.

sections.heading: Fat substitutes
paragraphs: Fat is a key component of ice cream, influencing texture, structure, melting behavior, and flavor (Wang et al.  76 ), according to Fig.  1 . Its presence supports desirable texture, shape retention, smoothness, foam stability, and restricts ice crystal formation (Wang et al.  76 ; Zhao et al.  80 ). Higher fat levels, with small droplets and particles, improve lubrication and creaminess, whereas fat reduction increases friction and decreases quality perception (Zhao et al.  80 ). Reducing fat content leads to defects such as coarseness, iciness, shrinkage, and flavor issues; for example, decreasing fat from 10 to 5% nearly doubled melting rate and reduced hardness and overrun (Zhao et al.  80 ). During churning and hardening, fat stabilizes air bubbles and limits ice crystals through fat globule coalescence, and its removal inevitably impairs quality (Wang et al.  77 ).

Fig. 1 Schematic representation of the role of fat in ice cream structure and quality attributes. Fat interacts with key elements of the matrix, such as air cells and ice crystals, and influences multiple properties including overrun, melting behavior, texture, structure, flavor, and stability. These effects are critical to maintaining the sensory and physical characteristics that define consumer acceptance of ice cream

Milk fat is composed mainly of saturated fatty acids (65–70%), whose excessive intake is associated with non-alcoholic cirrhosis and obesity (Wang et al.  77 ). Rising demand for healthier products has driven development of low-fat ice cream (Tolve et al.  74 ).

Fat reduction increases ice crystal size, reduces creaminess and smoothness, and accelerates melting because destabilized fat globules worsen structure (Yu et al.  79 ). Fat also carries flavor compounds; its reduction increases initial release but decreases persistence, as insufficient fat allows rapid volatilization, even with flavor addition (Genovese et al.  13 ).

Fat replacers, lipid-, protein-, or carbohydrate-based, can thicken, modify texture, and retain water (Zhao et al.  80 ). Polysaccharide blends (e.g., guar gum, locust bean gum) and whey protein can replicate creaminess and stability by increasing viscosity and smoothness (Zhao et al.  80 ). Microcrystalline cellulose and inulin also improve texture by limiting crystal growth (Tolve et al.  74 ). Saturated fat replacement strategies target calorie reduction, though protein- and carbohydrate-based substitutes may reduce fat-soluble flavors and shelf life (Qin et al.  57 ). Up to 25% fat replacement with 0.03 g/mL fiber can maintain texture (Hanafi et al.  22 ). However, some substitutes resist lipase hydrolysis, affecting digestion and causing intestinal effects (Qin et al.  57 ).

Effective replacers must replicate flavor release, texture, and functionality of milk fat (Genovese et al.  13 ). Several studies (Table  2 ) show that fat substitution can improve melting stability and hardness, for example, grapefruit nanocellulose, pea protein micro-gels, PFE, and soybean oil bodies enhance structure and stability (Qin et al.  57 ).

Table 2 Fat substitutes in ice cream Replacement level Category Application Effects on ice cream properties Sensory analysis Reference Partial (40–50% of milk fat) Oil-based Soybean oil body Improved stability through increased viscosity and reduced particle size. Comparable to control. (Wang et al.  76 ) Partial (15 to 7%) Fiber Grapefruit peel nanocellulose Increased hardness (59 to 136 N), improved shape retention and reduced melting rate (1.8 to 0.5%/min). Similar to control at 0.2–0.6% nanocellulose. (Yu et al.  79 ) Partial (2.5–12.5%) Oil-based Cold-pressed chia seed oil Comparable viscosity and rheology to full-fat ice cream. Similar acceptance to full-fat ice cream. (Atik et al.  3 ) Partial (9 to 6%) Fiber Inulin, acacia, apple, & oat fiber Similar to full fat with inulin; sensory altered with apple and oat fiber. Comparable for inulin; altered sensory for apple and oat. (Tolve et al.  74 ) Partial/Total (20–100%) Protein Pea protein micro-gels Comparable melting profile, overrun between 82.7 and 131%. Highest acceptance at 40–60% substitution. (Qin et al.  57 ) Partial/Total (25–100%) Protein Licorice extract & whey protein foam Reduced calories (167.43 to 48.37 kcal/100 g) and increased overrun (20.9 to 51.03%). Higher substitutions reduced acceptance; 25% comparable to control. (Nooshkam et al.  50 )

The use of soybean oil body replacements has been shown to improve viscosity and reduce particle size, resulting in enhanced stability (Wang et al.  77 ). These findings indicate that the structural contributions of plant-based or fiber-rich substitutes effectively emulate the stability of dairy fat. Overrun depends on the replacer: pea protein micro-gels can increase it substantially, while toasted corn powder and chia seed oil reduce it, leading to denser textures still accepted by consumers (Atik et al.  3 ). Sensory studies show that inulin, acacia fibers, saffron, and WPI can maintain desirable sensory properties (Tolve et al.  74 ). Moderate substitution with unripe banana biomass and pea protein micro-gels leads to high consumer acceptance (Qin et al.  57 ), whereas high substitution (e.g., licorice extract foam) reduces acceptance (Nooshkam et al.  50 ).

Some substitutes add antioxidant functionality, such as licorice extract and chia seed oil, appealing to health-focused consumers (Nooshkam et al.  50 ). Fiber-rich by-products like PFE and corn powder enhance texture and health attributes.
Increasingly, plant-based fibers and proteins are promising in partially replacing fat, enabling low-fat ice cream that balances sensory quality and functional stability.

sections.heading: Sugar substitutes
paragraphs: Sucrose is the most common and economical sweetener in ice cream, improving texture, palatability, viscosity, and flavor perception (Detoni et al.  10 ). Beyond sweetness, sugar influences the total solids and structural components of ice cream, ice crystals, air cells, and fat globules, dispersed in a partially frozen matrix (Romulo et al.  62 ). Sucrose and corn syrup solids are widely used to enhance body and texture while lowering the freezing point, reducing large ice crystal formation.

Growing interest in low-calorie products has driven substitution of sucrose with alternative sweeteners to reduce caloric content while maintaining product functionality (Genovese et al.  13 ). Sweeteners significantly influence physical and rheological properties, affecting consumer acceptance; for instance, stevia extract has shown positive effects when used as a replacement (Romulo et al.  62 ). Natural resources such as plant-based ingredients represent promising alternatives (Gheisari et al.  14 ).

Table  3  summarizes studies evaluating artificial and natural sucrose substitutes, detailing application, substitution level, outcomes, and references. These approaches may improve nutritional value, adding beneficial phytochemicals and valorizing plant and fermented products. Examples include honey in kefir ice cream (Januário et al.  31 ), and stevia leaf powder in goat milk ice cream (Robins et al.  60 ).

The highest level of acceptability was observed at a substitution ratio of 25% (Hassan et al.  25 ) Partial and total The effect of date ( Phoenix dactylifera)  versus sugar in ice cream properties All ice cream samples displayed 100% overrun, with no significant differences in fat content or density. Substituting sugar with date syrup increased the total phenol and anthocyanin content. Panelists preferred the ice cream containing 18% date syrup, and there were no statistically significant differences ( p  < 0.05) in overall reception (Gheisari et al.  14 ) Total Kefir ice cream flavored with fruits (lemon, guava, banana, and passion fruit) and sweetened with honey, compared with a pineapple commercial ice cream The lemon ice cream showed consistency and cohesiveness similar to that of the commercial product. The commercial ice cream had higher fat content and total solids compared to the Kefir ice cream. In the sensory analysis, all the ice creams (both Kefir and commercial) were well-received by the panelists, with the guava ice cream receiving the lowest scores (Januário et al.  31 ) Total Steviol glycosides and polydextrose as a bulking agent Caloric content decreased from 150 to 120 kcal per serving, but steviol glycosides received lower sensory scores, with panelists describing aftertastes as “artificial,” “bitter,” and “chemical” (Muenprasitivej et al.  49 )

Results vary, reflecting the complexity of maintaining ice cream quality after sucrose replacement. Honey substitution yielded kefir ice cream with similar consistency and cohesion to commercial products but reduced fat and total solids (Januário et al.  31 ). Goat milk ice cream with stevia had lower total solids and longer melting time yet good sensory acceptance (Robins et al.  60 ). However, sensory limitations, such as bitter or artificial notes from steviol glycosides, may reduce acceptance (Muenprasitivej et al.  49 ). Some substitutes provide functional benefits, including higher phenolic content and enzyme-inhibitory effects, as seen in ice cream with graviola pulp. Nevertheless, sensory acceptance remains a key challenge, and future work should seek a balance between nutritional/functional gains and sensory quality to ensure commercial success.

Although alternative sweeteners may improve the nutritional profile and introduce bioactive compounds, most reported functional benefits are based on compositional or in vitro analyses (Genovese et al.  13 ). Limited evidence is available regarding their metabolic effects in humans, particularly in the context of complex food matrices such as ice cream (Sarkar  66 ). Furthermore, the technological challenges associated with maintaining sensory quality often constrain their practical application (Soukoulis and Bohn  67 ).

sections.heading: Stabilizers and emulsifiers substitutes
paragraphs: The lack of stabilizers in ice cream leads to phase separation, with fat solidifying and water crystallizing; therefore, stabilizers and emulsifiers are essential for maintaining texture and consumer acceptability (Raisel et al.  58 ). Even in low concentrations, stabilizers increase viscosity, facilitate aeration, inhibit ice and lactose crystal growth, prevent shrinkage and moisture migration, support pumping and filling, and keep flavor particles suspended (Kozłowicz et al.  35 ; Detoni et al.  10 ; Raisel et al.  58 ).

Stabilizers and emulsifiers ensure proper structure (Fig.  2 ); emulsifiers such as mono- and diglycerides and polysorbates reduce interfacial tension and prevent droplet coalescence (Raisel et al.  58 ). Formulations commonly combine stabilizers, locust bean gum, guar gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, sodium alginate, gelatin, and secondary stabilizers like κ-carrageenan and pectin to avoid whey separation and maintain acidic stability (Roy et al.  63 ).
Fig. 2 Diagram showing the complementary roles of stabilizers and emulsifiers in ice cream, emphasizing their contributions to texture stability, emulsification, and consumer acceptability

Mono- and diglycerides remain primary emulsifiers, though alternatives are being explored (Loffredi and Alamprese  40 ). Polysorbate 80 enhances fat destabilization even at 0.01–0.03%, affecting meltdown and sensory properties (Warren and Hartel  78 ). Growing interest in clean-label products has encouraged using natural sources (vegetal/animal), legume proteins with emulsifying capacity, and phospholipids from milk, soy, or rice; many are obtained from by-products to increase sustainability (Loffredi and Alamprese  40 ).

Recent studies (Table  4 ) show wheat gluten modifications and vegetable/animal proteins (whey, lupin, rice) improve stability, melting time, overrun, and viscosity, though none surpass monoglycerides overall (Loffredi et al.  41 ). Citrus fiber, chia mucilage, and pomegranate/watermelon pectin enhance melting resistance and viscosity, though they may alter texture/flavor (Loffredi and Alamprese  40 ). Carrageenan and β-glucans reduce ice crystal size, increase density, and improve low-fat product stability (Raisel et al.  58 ; Roy et al.  63 ).

Table 4 The impact of emulsifiers and stabilizers on the aspects of ice creams Category Application Main findings Reference Algae derived stabilizer Alginate Adding 0.1% alginate boosts ice cream’s melting resistance, increasing melting time from 16.9 to 41.2 min. While overrun drops from 41.2% to 32.7%, viscosity and °Brix rise with higher alginate levels. Panelists rated the texture and acceptability better, at 6.2 compared to 5 in the control, demonstrating alginate’s effectiveness in enhancing stability and texture. (Nuary et al.  52 ) Animal and vegetal protein and oligosaccharide blend Citrus fiber, α-cyclodextrin, and whey protein concentrate. A blend of α-cyclodextrin, whey protein concentrate, and citrus fiber maintained similar physical properties to the control, mimicking its firmness and melting while ensuring high stability. (Loffredi and Alamprese  40 ) Animal based emulsifier Chicken and Duck egg Duck eggs improved color, aroma, and taste; chicken egg enhanced softness and meltability. (Octaliandra and Holinesti  54 ) Animal protein derived emulsifier Milk protein concentrate (MPC) and milk protein reduced calcium (RCMPC) The addition of MPC and RCMPC boosted protein content and viscosity without affecting consistency. RCMPC proved more effective in preventing shrinkage, enhancing structural integrity over time, and maintaining stability after 180 days at concentrations of 1% or higher. (Paglia et al.  55 ) Animal protein-based emulsifier Ultrafiltered sweet butter whey Ice cream with 5% buttermilk (S4) showed increased hardness, consistency, overrun (35.8%), and reduced melting time, though flavor, color, and aroma were less preferred. Butter content reduced the melting index, highlighting the structural role of phospholipids, but excessive sweet butter whey may affect taste. The best sensory acceptance was observed at 0.8%. (Kozłowicz et al.  35 ) Plant based emulsifier Modified wheat gluten Improved the overrun and meltdown rates when compared with monoglycerides and soy protein isolates, and it was favorable sensory scores by consumers. (Pei et al.  56 ) Polysaccharide and protein blend Guar gum, sahlep and quince seed extract powder (QSEP) Guar gum extended melting time (3781 s) with the lowest overrun (26.83%). QSEP increased phenolic content (22.07 mg GAE/100 g). Sahlep had the shortest melting time but the highest sensory rating, followed by the QSEP-sahlep blend. (Demir and Arslan  9 ) Polysaccharide based stabilizer Kappa-carrageenan gum (KGC) in high protein ice cream The KCG stabilizer significantly improves the quality of high-protein ice cream. At 0.12%, it enhances melting resistance, achieves overrun beyond 100%, and reduces hardness. However, the optimal balance of sensory properties is found at a concentration of 0.06%. (Roy et al.  63 ) Starch based stabilizer Annealed Bambara  Starch The sample had taste, aroma, color, viscosity, and overrun similar to conventional ice cream but showed lower melting resistance after a 45 °C heat treatment. It offered excellent appearance, higher consumer acceptance, and better economic benefits. (Raisel et al.  58 ) Yeast derived emulsifier Mannoprotein bio emulsifier from  Saccharomyces cerevisiae At 0.2%, mannoprotein enhances stability, improves melt resistance, and achieves sensory acceptance comparable to commercial emulsifiers, making it an effective bio emulsifier for ice cream. (Thraeib et al.  73 )

Ingredients like alginate, microalgae, and oleogels increase nutritional value and stability but may impact sensory acceptance (Nuary et al.  52 ). Blending synthetic and natural stabilizers such as guar gum, tapioca fiber, and cellulose can produce better sensory acceptance than commercial stabilizers (Raisel et al.  58 ). Natural options improve sustainability yet still struggle to match synthetic stabilizer performance; optimized blends and approaches like polysaccharides and oleogel are promising (Loffredi and Alamprese  40 ). Solid content increases with water retention capacity of stabilizers (Nuary et al.  52 ).

Despite increasing consumer demand for natural ingredients, synthetic stabilizers remain more consistent and cost-efficient (Raisel et al.  58 ). Added red algae, minerals, or microalgae can enhance nutrition but may lack sensory richness; combining them with fats or protein-based stabilizers ensures balance (Markowska et al.  44 ). Stabilizers such as guar or konjac gum effectively maintain structure but may require flavor enhancement to meet sensory expectations.

sections.heading: Supplements
paragraphs: Food components with functional properties can serve as natural additives, enhancing the nutritional profile of ice cream through the incorporation of dietary fibers, phenolic compounds, natural pigments, and flavoring agents (Genovese et al.  13 ). Although traditionally perceived as an indulgent and less healthy product, ice cream may contribute positively to sensory experiences, particularly among older adults, due to its cooling effect and appealing texture contrast. In this context, the incorporation of nutraceutical compounds, including prebiotics, antioxidants, phenolics, dietary fibers, and other natural ingredients, has emerged as a key strategy in the development of healthier ice cream formulations (Sarkar  66 ). Alternative sources, such as fruit by-products, particularly peels, have attracted attention due to their high bioactive content, although their use may also introduce challenges related to color, texture, and sensory acceptance (Tarchi et al.  70 ). At the same time, increasing consumer concern regarding synthetic additives has accelerated the replacement of artificial colorants with natural pigments that offer both visual and functional benefits.

Among functional strategies, probiotics, defined as live microorganisms that confer health benefits when consumed in adequate amounts (Sabet-Sarvestani et al.  64 ), have been widely incorporated into dairy-based matrices. Ice cream is considered a suitable carrier due to its relatively neutral pH, favorable nutrient composition, and sensory acceptance (Janipour et al.  30 ). Moreover, milk constituents can protect probiotic viability during freezing and storage, while the addition of natural flavors further supports consumer acceptance (Detoni et al.  10 ). In parallel, prebiotic oligosaccharides such as lactulose, fructooligosaccharides (FOS), and galactooligosaccharides (GOS) have gained attention due to their ability to selectively stimulate beneficial gut microbiota and improve metabolic and mineral absorption functions (Sarkar  66 ).

These compounds may also influence technological properties, contributing to sweetness, freezing behavior, and texture, and can partially replace sugar or fat (Genovese et al.  13 ; Mohammed et al.  47 ). However, their effects are concentration-dependent, and excessive incorporation may result in undesirable sensory changes and potential gastrointestinal discomfort. In this context, symbiotic systems combining probiotics and prebiotics have been investigated to enhance functional outcomes (Sabet-Sarvestani et al.  64 ).

Beyond ingredient incorporation, several technological strategies have been explored to improve the functional quality of ice cream, including process optimization, genetic approaches, and the application of nano- and microencapsulation Technologies (Hari et al.  23 ). These advanced systems have shown significant potential to enhance the stability, bioaccessibility, and bioavailability of bioactive compounds by protecting them from degradation during processing and storage. In addition, nano-formulations may improve sensory characteristics by masking undesirable flavors and enabling controlled release of active compounds. For instance, nanoencapsulation of lipophilic bioactives such as carotenoids and essential oils improves dispersion and stability within dairy matrices (Augustin and Sanguansri  4 ; McClements  45 ), while encapsulated omega-3 fatty acids and plant extracts exhibit enhanced oxidative stability and sensory acceptance (Jafari et al.  29 ; Gowda et al.  20 ). Furthermore, these systems can influence physical properties, including increased viscosity and improved melting resistance, due to their interaction with the ice cream matrix (Soukoulis et al.  68 ; Hari et al.  23 ). Nevertheless, their industrial application remains limited by cost, scalability, and regulatory constraints (McClements  45 ).

However, the successful incorporation of bioactive compounds does not necessarily ensure their physiological effectiveness, as this depends largely on their bioaccessibility and bioavailability. Bioaccessibility refers to the fraction of a compound released from the food matrix during digestion, whereas bioavailability involves its absorption and biological utilization. The multiphase structure of ice cream, particularly its fat content and emulsified system, may enhance the protection and delivery of lipophilic bioactives. For example, fat globules and emulsifiers can facilitate the solubilization of carotenoids and polyphenols, improving intestinal absorption. Conversely, interactions with proteins and polysaccharides, as well as processing conditions such as freezing and storage, may limit compound stability and release. Although several studies report enhanced antioxidant activity and probiotic viability, these in vitro findings do not necessarily translate into in vivo health benefits (Genovese et al.  13 ; Sarkar  66 ).

In addition, the food matrix plays a crucial role in modulating the bioaccessibility and bioavailability of incorporated bioactive compounds. Interactions between proteins, lipids, and polysaccharides within the ice cream system may either enhance or hinder the release and absorption of these compounds during digestion (Soukoulis and Bohn  67 ; McClements  45 ). As a result, the mere incorporation of bioactives does not guarantee their functional efficacy, reinforcing the importance of integrating digestion models and bioavailability studies into future research.

Despite the increasing number of studies reporting functional improvements in ice cream formulations, the scientific evidence supporting these health benefits remains inconsistent and heterogeneous (Genovese et al.  13 ; Sarkar  66 ). Many reported effects, such as antioxidant capacity and enzyme inhibition, are based on in vitro assays, which do not necessarily represent physiological conditions in humans.

Although in vivo studies, especially in animal models, provide additional indications of potential benefits such as anti-inflammatory or chemopreventive effects, their translation to human health is still limited (Sarkar  66 ). Furthermore, there is a lack of well-controlled clinical trials evaluating the long-term effects of functional ice cream consumption. Therefore, caution is required when extrapolating these results to functional claims, emphasizing the need for more robust human-based clinical evidence to validate the proposed health benefits.

Within this framework, the incorporation of lipids such as omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) has gained attention due to their cardiovascular and anti-inflammatory benefits. Enrichment using sources like chia and flaxseed oils can improve nutritional value, but outcomes depend on formulation strategies. Ullah et al. ( 75 ) observed increased omega-3 content but reported oxidative instability as a key limitation, while Gowda et al. ( 20 ) showed that microencapsulation can enhance stability and sensory quality. More complex systems combining omega-3s with prebiotics and probiotics have also been proposed, with potential synergistic effects but increased formulation complexity (Lai et al.  38 ). Overall, these studies highlight that technological approaches are essential to ensure both stability and functional efficacy.

Table  5  summarizes studies on ice cream fortification with functional ingredients, including probiotics, prebiotics, natural colorants, and other bioactive compounds. Probiotic strains such as  Lactobacillus casei  and  Bifidobacterium BB-12 , as well as prebiotics like fructooligosaccharides and ora-pro-nobis, have been shown to improve gut microbiota and antioxidant activity (Santos et al.  65 ). Additionally, bioactive systems containing β-carotene and vitamin nanophytosomes combined with anise oil may provide health benefits, including protective effects on liver and kidney function, reinforcing ice cream as a functional food matrix (Hari et al.  23 ).

Carotenoids from natural sources such as carrot, pumpkin, and microalgae are increasingly explored due to their dual role in coloration and nutritional enhancement. Carrot and pumpkin pulps increase β-carotene content and antioxidant capacity, although excessive levels may negatively affect rheology and sensory acceptance (Rajarajan  59 ). Similarly, microalgae like  Spirulina  enhance antioxidant properties but may introduce strong coloration and off-flavors (Moharam et al.  48 ).

Natural colorants such as phycocyanin from  Spirulina  further support clean-label strategies, improving visual appeal and potentially contributing to texture and structural stability. In addition to its coloring function, phycocyanin has been shown to influence ice cream structure (Rodrigues et al.  61 ) and remain stable under frozen storage for up to 90 days (Mendonça et al.  46 ).

Despite these advances, consumer acceptance remains a major challenge. Functional ingredients such as coconut fiber and  Lactobacillus  strains may reduce acceptability due to undesirable changes in taste and texture (Hanafi et al.  22 ), while unconventional colors from natural pigments (e.g., green or blue) may negatively influence purchase intention (Lučan Čolić et al.  42 ). Therefore, the successful development of functional ice cream depends on balancing nutritional enhancement, technological performance, and sensory acceptance.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future perspectives
paragraphs: Ice cream is transitioning from an indulgent dessert to a potential functional food vehicle, enabled by the use of dairy and plant-based ingredients, natural sweeteners, fat replacers, and emulsifiers that aim to improve nutritional quality while maintaining acceptable sensory properties. However, balancing health-oriented reformulation with consumer acceptance remains a central challenge, particularly regarding taste and texture.

To overcome these limitations, strategies such as sensory and rheological analyses, hybrid formulations combining plant and animal ingredients, flavor-masking techniques, and statistical optimization tools are being applied. The use of regional plant materials, agro-industrial by-products, and tailored formulations for specific populations also supports more sustainable and targeted product development.

Despite progress, many functional claims are still based on preliminary evidence, highlighting the need for clinical validation and standardized testing methods. Future research should integrate technological innovation with robust sensory and consumer studies to ensure both product quality and scientifically proven health benefits.
Overall, the development of functional ice creams is feasible, but optimizing sensory quality while confirming functional efficacy remains a key scientific and technological challenge.
